title: Airbnb Just Popped After a Blowout Quarter. Is the Stock Still a Buy?

Airbnb Just Popped After a Blowout Quarter. Is the Stock Still a Buy?
Matt Frankel, CFP®, The Motley Fool
Sat, November 7, 2026 at 7:02 AM CST 5 min read
ABNB
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase

Airbnb (NASDAQ:ABNB) shares jumped by 12% on Friday after the company reported third-quarter results that handily beat expectations. The stock is now just under its 52-week high and has gained 40% so far in 2026.

For the past few years, the general consensus among investors has been that Airbnb is a great business. It's just not growing at a rate that anyone would consider impressive. But the company's third-quarter results could change that perception.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

A blowout quarter with a lot to like

Airbnb's revenue grew 19% year-over-year, or 16% excluding any currency effects, which was significantly higher than analysts were expecting. On the bottom line, earnings per share were $3.16, compared to the $2.85 expectation among Wall Street analysts.

Demand was extremely strong as well. Nights and seats booked through the platform reached 155 million, up 16% from a year ago, and gross booking value grew 21% to $27.7 billion. Plus, the company remains an absolute cash machine. Airbnb has generated $4.9 billion in free cash flow over the past 12 months, and adjusted EBITDA increased by 22%.

The company is also starting to explore new growth areas and gain traction in some. Airbnb recently began adding adjacent services such as meal delivery and car rentals, and traditional hotels now account for a significant (but still single-digit) share of booked nights. These are all small pieces of Airbnb's revenue today, but they provide Airbnb with credible pathways to maintaining an elevated growth rate.

Looking ahead, management expects Airbnb's fourth-quarter revenue to fall in the range of $3.22-$3.28 billion, representing 17% growth at the midpoint.

Putting its cash to work

Airbnb has over $12 billion in cash on its balance sheet and, as mentioned, is generating free cash flow of roughly $5 billion annually. Well, the board authorized a new $12 billion share repurchase program, and that's on top of the $2.7 billion left under the existing authorization. Even after Friday's pop, the new buyback alone represents more than 10% of Airbnb's market value.

It's worth noting that Airbnb uses these buybacks (in part) to offset dilution from stock-based compensation, and the share count has shrunk and should continue to do so.

Over the past year, Booking Holdings (BKNG) stock lost 17.5%, dividends included, compared with a 9.8% return for the S&P 500. This performance marked the worst return within a peer group of five that includes Meta Platforms, Airbnb, Expedia and Hyatt Hotels. The lag occurred even though Meta is the only company in the group that converts a larger share of sales into operating profit than Booking does. So what do Booking's rivals offer that Booking does not?

Booking Is More Profitable Than Airbnb But Grows Slower

Most competitors offer faster sales growth. Airbnb operates in the same hotel and resort industry and provides the starkest contrast. During the four fiscal quarters ended September 30, 2026, Booking retained 32.8% of its revenue as operating profit, compared with 22.5% at Airbnb. Yet Booking reported revenue growth of 8.0% over those quarters, which is about half of Airbnb's 16.7% pace. That figure is held down by a $900 million legal charge, linked to an FTC action, that cut third-quarter revenue.

Investors pay far less for that profit, pricing the stock at 16.8 times earnings compared with 34.9 for Airbnb. Meta Platforms generates nearly the exact same margin as Booking, but its revenue expanded 27.5%. Meta is the only other comparable company priced above Booking on an earnings basis. Shares of Airbnb (NASDAQ:ABNB) leaped more than 11% on Friday after the online lodging marketplace said its pace of expansion was quickening.

Image source: Getty Images.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

More people are turning to Airbnb for their rental needs

Airbnb's revenue climbed 19% year over year to $4.9 billion in the third quarter.

Nights and seats booked on its platform rose 16% to 155 million, driving a 21% rise in gross booking value to $27.7 billion.

"It's rare for a marketplace of our size to reaccelerate growth, but that's exactly what we're doing," CEO Brian Chesky said. "In Q3, we delivered our fastest revenue growth in more than three years, with acceleration across our business, including our most established markets."

Chesky said Airbnb has redesigned its app to make it easier to find and book a home. "Our growth isn't being driven by any single product or feature," Chesky said. "It's the result of hundreds of improvements we've made across Airbnb over the last several years."

Notably, more people are making their first transaction on Airbnb's platform. First-time booker growth rose 13%. Younger, Gen Z customers were the company's fastest-growing cohort.

Airbnb is rewarding investors with larger cash returns

All told, Airbnb's free cash flow soared 29% to $1.4 billion in the third quarter and 35% to $4.9 billion over the trailing 12 months.

This impressive cash generation enabled Airbnb to announce a $12 billion stock buyback program, as it moves to return more capital to shareholders

Healthy global travel demand trends also prompted Airbnb to lift its full-year revenue target. Management now projects a revenue growth rate in the "high teens" with further profit margin expansion.

For investors holding Booking Holdings (BKNG), the rise of AI assistants raises questions about the future of a business built on helping travelers find accommodations. Travelers are still booking more for now, with room nights rising 7% in the third quarter of 2026, up from 5% in the second. Yet a sharper form of that worry surfaced on Booking's November 3 earnings call. What is that worry, and how far has it reached?

Could Travelers Book Through AI Instead Of Booking?

This scenario could unfold if AI agents that plan and book trips direct users to hotel websites instead of online travel agencies like Booking. Should this happen at scale, a traveler could secure a room without ever opening Booking.com.

So far, AI remains a small channel for Booking. Management said referrals from AI chatbots still bring in well under 1% of Booking.com's room nights. Booking is also working with OpenAI, expanding paid referrals into more markets.

How Much Of Booking's Business Could AI Reach?

In principle, the worry extends to the entire $28.1 billion of revenue Booking reported over the twelve months to September 2026, as the issue centers on how travelers discover the platform in the first place. That revenue figure climbed 8.0% from a year earlier, a slower pace than the 13.0% growth recorded over the preceding twelve months. For the third quarter, reported revenue was 1.3% below a year earlier, reflecting a $900 million reduction tied to a pending FTC matter at Priceline, while management put adjusted revenue, its own measure, up 9%.

Travelers still come straight to Booking, however. The share of its consumer room nights booked directly held steady in the mid-60% range over the past four quarters. At the same time, the mobile app's share of room nights increased to the high-50% range, up from the mid-50% range a year earlier.

Booking.com also does not depend on major hotel chains. Independent hotels and alternative accommodation partners generate the vast majority of its room nights, and the ten largest global hotel chains account for only a low double-digit percentage. On the call, management said partners pay nothing unless a guest books, and that it believes Booking holds an advantage. The company has also launched its own AI travel agent, Vayo, backed by a planned $100 million investment.

Management cannot yet say how fast AI agents will catch on. It said referrals from AI chatbots have picked up over the last several weeks, and also noted that the rules on personal data and payments are complex. It added that these agents may spread much more slowly than expected in parts of the world, and that it does not know what that will mean for Booking itself.

Stocks closed out a volatile week on a relatively quiet note as market participants caught their breath after Thursday's broad-based beatdown.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite made a valiant attempt at a rebound as several tech stocks bounced, but Friday's gains put just a small dent in its weekly decline. Moves by the broader S&P 500 and blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average were far less impressive.

At the close, the Nasdaq was up 1.1% at 24,579 — still in correction territory, but paring its week-over-week deficit to 3.4%. The S&P 500 finished the day up 0.3% at 7,376, and the week down 2.7%. And the Dow slipped 0.5% Friday to 51,285, and was 0.9% lower on the week.

Markets sold off sharply Thursday on concerns that Democratic leadership in Washington and several states, from Texas to Ohio, will create headwinds for the data center buildout.

Several tech stocks that were hit the hardest on Thursday swung higher on Friday, including memory chipmaker Micron Technology (MU, +5.1%) and artificial intelligence (AI) bellwether Nvidia (NVDA, +2.8%).

Questions Answered

Question

	

Answer

	

Evidence




Is growth really reaccelerating?

	

Yes

	

Revenue $4.87B vs $4.75B est, up 19% YoY, the fastest in over three years




Is it just a pricing effect?

	

Mostly not

	

Nights & Seats Booked rose 16% to 155M, from about 10% in Q2. Canaccord estimates about 13% excluding a 3-point lift from Reserve Now, Pay Later.




Is it broad-based?

	

Yes

	

All major regions accelerated, and first-time bookers hit their strongest pace in several years (Jefferies).




Can profitability hold?

	

Yes

	

EBITDA was $2.51B at a 52% margin. FY2026 margin guidance was lifted to about 36%.




Is the industry weakness hitting Airbnb?

	

Not so far

	

Booking Holdings, Expedia and TripAdvisor flagged higher airfares and European unrest. Airbnb guided above the Street.

EPS was $3.16 vs $2.85 est (+10.9%). Gross booking value rose 21% to $27.7B. FY2026 revenue growth guidance moved to "high teens" from "at least mid-teens". That is the third consecutive raise.

Unsure what to buy ahead of earnings? Our AI's recent pre-earnings calls delivered gains of +77% to +118% after results dropped. See this month's earnings picks »

Earnings history shows a clear turn. EPS missed in Q4 2025 (-15%) and Q1 2026 (-16%). Then it beat in Q2 (+8.7%, stock +16.8%) and Q3.

Caveats Still Open

Guidance assumes calm. It excludes any persistent hit from unrest in France or the Middle East conflict.

Q4 growth moderates. Nights Booked growth faces tougher comparisons, and EBITDA margin dips slightly YoY as marketing spend shifts into Q4.

Valuation is rich. Cantor (Neutral, $180 target) cites about 27x FY2027 P/E. InvestingPro shows a trailing P/E of 38.5. Evercore's comparison is 14x for Booking Holdings and 11x for Expedia.

The stock has already run. It is +58.4% over 1 year and +19% over 1 month (as of Nov 6).

Part of the boost is mechanical. Reserve Now, Pay Later expansion contributed to the Nights Booked acceleration.

Next Catalysts

Q4 guidance delivery. Revenue guidance is $3.22B–$3.28B vs the $3.16B Street estimate. Q4 results are expected around Feb 16, 2027 (tentative). Consensus is EPS $0.85 and revenue $3.16B, and it will likely rise.

$12B buyback. The new authorization compares with $12.6B of cash and short-term investments at Sep 30. It gives a floor of support.

AI Travel Agent. Launch is planned for the first half of 2027, with broader "agentic experiences" next year. Mizuho calls ABNB its top internet pick and sets a $245 target, the Street high.

Hotels and services. Hotels are growing "markedly faster" than the core rental business but remain a single-digit share of revenue. There is also a new American Express partnership and car rentals.

Estimate revisions. Consensus EPS is $5.31 for FY2026 and $6.26 for FY2027. Revisions over 90 days are only +1.6%, so there is room to catch up.

Macro risks. Airfares and European unrest could undermine the "no material impact" assumption.
